title: The Ruined Loincloth and the Wineskins
summary: God has Jeremiah buy a linen loincloth, wear it, and then bury it in a cleft of rock at Perath, and when he digs it up many days later it is ruined. God explains that Judah, meant to cling to him like that garment, has become just as useless through pride. A proverb about wineskins, a plea to give glory to God before darkness falls, a word to the king and queen mother, and a closing poem of shame and exile complete the chapter.
story: The chapters before this one announced judgment in speech. Here Jeremiah acts it out. This is the first of several sign-acts in the book (a smashed jar in chapter 19, a yoke in chapter 27, a field purchase in chapter 32), in which the prophet's body and possessions become part of the message. The chapter moves from a private enactment to a public warning and finally to the palace itself, as the king and the queen mother are told their crowns have fallen. The shape of the whole story is here in miniature: a people chosen to be close to God, a pride that spoils them, and an exile that will strip away everything they trusted.
historical:
Verse 18 addresses "the king and to the queen mother", and most interpreters identify them as King Jehoiachin and his mother Nehushta. Jehoiachin came to the throne at eighteen in 598 or 597 BC, reigned three months, and surrendered to Nebuchadnezzar in 597 BC, when he, his mother, and his officials were taken to Babylon (2 Kings 24:8-15; Jeremiah 22:26 and 29:2 also name the queen mother). Verse 19, "All Judah has been carried into exile", could describe that deportation as it happened, or it could be prophetic language that speaks of a certain future as already done. The foe "from the north" (verse 20) is Babylon.

The location of "Perath" is debated. The Hebrew word is the usual name for the Euphrates River, roughly 350 miles from Jerusalem, which would make Jeremiah's two round trips a matter of months on the road. Others note a village called Parah in Benjamin (Joshua 18:23), a few miles from Jeremiah's home at Anathoth, where a spring still bears a related name; a short walk there would have made the act visible to local watchers while the name still pointed toward the Euphrates and Babylon. A third view takes the whole account as a vision. The text does not settle it, and its meaning is the same on each reading.
cultural:
A loincloth (or waistband) was the garment worn closest to the body, wrapped around the hips. Linen was the material of priestly clothing (Leviticus 16:4), so a linen garment may hint at Israel's calling to be a priestly people. Keeping it out of water may mean it was new and unwashed, or it may prepare for the contrast with its later rot in damp ground. Verse 11 draws the lesson: the garment clings to a man as Israel was meant to cling to God, "for My renown and praise and glory". A garment is honor to the one who wears it, and a ruined one is disgrace.

The queen mother (Hebrew gebirah) held a recognized office in Judah. The books of Kings name the mother of nearly every Judean king, and some queen mothers wielded real power, like Maacah, whom King Asa removed for making an idol (1 Kings 15:13). Wineskins were leather or clay jars; the Hebrew here can mean either. The people's reply in verse 12 treats Jeremiah's saying as a truism, which sets up the twist: the drunkenness God pours out is the stupor of judgment, leaving a nation unable to act wisely as it staggers into disaster. The "Ethiopian" of verse 23 is a Cushite, from the kingdom south of Egypt along the upper Nile, whose people were known in Judah as soldiers and traders (Ebed-melech, who later rescues Jeremiah, is one).
literary: The chapter is a collection of five units bound together by the theme of pride. The sign-act (verses 1 to 11) follows a pattern repeated three times: the LORD speaks, Jeremiah obeys ("So I went"), and the meaning is finally given. The wineskin saying (verses 12 to 14) uses a proverb and a question to set up a reversal. Verses 15 to 17 are a short poem of warning ending in the prophet's private tears. Verses 18 and 19 are a funeral song for the royal house, and verses 20 to 27 address Jerusalem as a woman, first a shepherdess who has lost her flock and then an unfaithful wife exposed in public. The words for pride and for being "of no use at all" recur, tying the enacted sign to the spoken oracles.

outline.t: The linen loincloth buried and ruined
Every wineskin filled: the drunkenness of judgment
Give glory to God before the darkness
A lament for the king and queen mother

doctrines.note: Israel was made to "cling" to God as a garment clings to its wearer, so that its life would bring him praise. The covenant was a closeness meant to display God to the world.

Verse 23 is one of the Bible's bleakest statements of human bondage: those "accustomed to doing evil" cannot change themselves any more than a leopard can change its spots. Sin is shown as a settled habit of the heart, not a series of slips.
Pride is the charge that runs through the chapter. Judgment here is God removing what a proud people trusted until only shame remains.

words.note: Ezor, a loincloth or waistband, the garment tied around the hips. It appears eight times in this chapter. It was an intimate, everyday piece of clothing, which is exactly the point: God chose a garment worn close to the body as the picture of how near Israel was meant to be to him.

Davaq, to cling, cleave, or stick fast. It is the verb of Genesis 2:24, where a man holds fast to his wife, and of Deuteronomy's call to hold fast to the LORD. In verse 11 it describes both the garment's closeness to the body and God's purpose for Israel, so the image of the loincloth carries the language of marriage and covenant loyalty.

Gebirah, lady or mistress, used here for the queen mother. In Judah this was an official position with influence at court. By naming her alongside the king, the oracle addresses the whole royal house, and the crowns that fall in verse 18 belong to both.

christ: The chapter's central image, a people made to cling to God for his praise and glory, finds its fulfillment in Jesus, who is the faithful Israelite who does cling to the Father and whose life gives God glory without failure (John 17:4). The link is thematic rather than predictive. Verse 23 names a problem that the rest of Jeremiah answers: a people who cannot change their own hearts will be given new ones. Jeremiah promises a new covenant with the law written on the heart (31:33), and the New Testament proclaims that this is what Christ's death and the gift of the Spirit accomplish (Hebrews 8:8-12; 2 Corinthians 5:17). The prophet's secret weeping over the LORD's captive flock (verse 17) also anticipates Jesus weeping over the same city (Luke 19:41).

hard.q: How should we read the images of a woman stripped and exposed in verses 22 and 26?
hard.a: Many readers find these verses disturbing, and they should not be passed over. The prophets often pictured Jerusalem as God's wife and her idolatry as adultery (Hosea 2, Ezekiel 16 and 23), and they drew on the ancient practice of publicly shaming an unfaithful woman and on the real horrors that invading armies inflicted on captured cities. Some scholars argue that the imagery reflects and risks reinforcing violence against women and must be read critically. Others stress that the figure is a city and its leaders (who were men), that the metaphor is meant to shock the male elite by casting them as the disgraced party, and that the exposure describes what conquest would actually do. Both observations can be true at once. The text is describing the consequence of betrayal in the harshest terms available to it; it does not license any person to treat another this way, and the same book pictures God as a husband grieving to take his bride back (3:12-14; 31:3-4).

questions: God says he made Israel cling to him like a garment, for his praise. What would it look like for your life to be that close to God?
Verse 23 says people accustomed to evil cannot simply change themselves. Where have you found that to be true, and what hope does the rest of Scripture offer?
Jeremiah says he will weep in secret over the people's pride. How do you respond to the failures of people you are responsible for: with anger, distance, or grief?
